lineage_context.teaching_goal: Recognize the opposite-node + distinct calyx/corolla + capsule architecture as the more 'conventional flower' pathway within Caryophyllales.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first module centered on opposite leaves, swollen nodes, free petals and capsular fruit, with Paronychia exception
project_scope.note: Paronychia is a useful exception: conspicuous scarious stipules and one-seeded utricle-type fruit mean the learner must not make 'many-seeded capsule' absolute.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Look at the node: leaves are usually opposite, often joined at the base, and the node may be swollen. Then inspect the flower for 4–5 sepals plus 4–5 usually free petals and a superior ovary; the fruit is commonly a many-seeded capsule opening by teeth or valves.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly herbs. Leaves simple, usually opposite and entire; adjacent leaf bases may be connate. Nodes are often swollen. Stipules are absent in many genera but conspicuous and scarious in Paronychia.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers usually bisexual and radial. Sepals usually 4–5, free or fused; petals usually 4–5, free and often clawed/notched or deeply bifid.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a many-seeded capsule opening at the top by teeth or valves; Paronychia and some relatives are important one-seeded utricle exceptions.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Family door: opposite leaves + swollen/connate node + obvious free petals + capsule. Then check whether you are in a Silene/Stellaria-type capsule lineage or the stipulate Paronychia exception.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: opposite node → sepals+free petals → capsule teeth/valves → genus doors → Paronychia exception
visual_lesson.intro: Caryophyllaceae looks like the most 'normal flower' of this Caryophyllales batch: opposite leaves, separate sepals and petals, and usually a many-seeded capsule.

steps.title: 1 · Start at the opposite swollen node
steps.look_for: Pairs of simple leaves at the same node; bases may join around the stem and the node may look distinctly swollen.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a fast vegetative clue against Polygonaceae's ocrea and Amaranthaceae's more variable leaf arrangement.

steps.title: 2 · Separate calyx from corolla
steps.look_for: A real calyx and a separate petal whorl; petals are often free, clawed, notched or split.
steps.why_it_matters: This clean two-whorl flower contrasts strongly with Nyctaginaceae's one petaloid perianth and Amaranthaceae's tiny tepals.

steps.title: 3 · Follow the flower into the capsule
steps.look_for: A dry capsule containing many small seeds, opening at the top by teeth or valves.
steps.why_it_matters: Capsule dehiscence is a major family confirmation character.

steps.title: 4 · Silene/Saponaria door: tubular calyx + clawed petals
steps.look_for: A fused or tubular calyx surrounding long-clawed petals; mature capsule opens by apical teeth.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the classic campion/soapwort pattern.

steps.title: 5 · Stellaria/Cerastium/Arenaria door: small white star flowers
steps.look_for: Small white 5-petaled flowers; Stellaria petals are often so deeply bifid they look like ten, while Cerastium and Arenaria use petal/capsule details to split further.
steps.why_it_matters: These common-looking little white flowers become tractable once you inspect petal division and capsule teeth.

steps.title: 6 · Paronychia exception: scarious stipules + utricle
steps.photo_role: silvery stipules at opposite node + tiny flowers
steps.look_for: Opposite leaves connected by conspicuous white/silvery scarious stipules; tiny flowers may lack true petals and the fruit is a one-seeded utricle rather than a typical many-seeded capsule.
steps.why_it_matters: This prevents an overly rigid family rule and explains why Paronychia can look surprisingly unlike Silene.

comparisons.title: Caryophyllaceae vs Amaranthaceae
comparisons.rule: Caryophyllaceae usually has opposite leaves, distinct sepals and petals, and many-seeded capsules. Amaranthaceae usually has tiny one-whorl flowers with papery bracts and one-seeded fruits.

comparisons.title: Caryophyllaceae vs Polygonaceae
comparisons.rule: Caryophyllaceae lacks the classic ocrea and usually has opposite leaves; Polygonaceae commonly has an ocrea and a one-seeded angled nut.

comparisons.title: Caryophyllaceae vs Nyctaginaceae
comparisons.rule: Caryophyllaceae usually has true sepals + petals and a capsule; Nyctaginaceae has one petaloid perianth and an anthocarp around a one-seeded fruit.

comparisons.title: Caryophyllaceae vs Portulacaceae and Talinaceae
comparisons.rule: Do not use five petals or opposite leaves alone. Portulaca usually has two sepals and a capsule opening around its middle by a lid (circumscissile pyxis); Talinum usually has two sepals and a capsule splitting lengthwise. Many typical Caryophyllaceae capsules open at the tip by teeth or valves, but Paronychia bears a one-seeded utricle.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not make petals or many-seeded capsules universal. Paronychia and other paronychioid lineages can have petal-like staminodes or no petals and one-seeded utricles.
